passage:
“So which side are you on, Yamini?” Devika asked in the corridor outside the design studio, two of her teammates behind her.
“Neither. I just want the brand launch to go well.”
“Neutral means you're with them,” Devika said.
An hour later Karan, the creative head, caught Yamini at the printer. “Devika's people have been moving your files. Where will you sit at the offsite?”
“With both teams, I hope.”
Karan shrugged. On Friday, when a delay was pinned on “people who avoid commitment,” neither camp spoke up. Only Farid, the quiet senior designer, said, “Yamini sent her part on Tuesday. I have the email.” Yamini looked at him, surprised.

qa.q: What did Karan say Devika's people had been doing?
qa.a: Karan said Devika's people had been moving Yamini's files.

qa.q: Why did Yamini answer, “Neither. I just want the brand launch to go well”?
qa.a: Yamini wants to stay out of the rival camps and believes the work matters more, though the answer leaves both sides suspicious.

qa.q: What helped Yamini when the delay was blamed on “people who avoid commitment”?
qa.a: A quiet ally, Farid, spoke up with the email showing Yamini had sent her part on time, which protected Yamini when neither camp did.

qa.q: How might Devika have seen Yamini's “Neither”?
qa.a: Devika seems to read it as taking the other side, since Devika said, “Neutral means you're with them.”

grounding: An employee tries to stay out of rival camps, is pressed by both, and is protected only by a quiet ally.

passage: I'm Sachin, and for two years I told myself neutrality was a virtue. Our department had two camps, one loyal to Hemant, the regional head, the other to the operations director. Both kept asking me for news about the other. I gave each the same polite answer: “I only do my job.” It felt principled. Then a shipment went wrong, and each camp assumed I'd told the other side. Hemant stopped copying me on mails. The director's team stopped inviting me to lunch. When the review came, nobody defended me because nobody thought I was theirs. Only Bhavna, from stores, said quietly, “The records are clean. I checked them.” Looking back, I needed a couple of people like that before things went wrong.

qa.q: What polite answer did Sachin give both camps?
qa.a: Sachin said, “I only do my job.”

qa.q: Why did Sachin see neutrality as a virtue?
qa.a: Sachin felt principled and comfortable staying out of both camps, without seeing that neutrality left no one to speak up for Sachin.

qa.q: What might Sachin have done earlier to avoid being squeezed?
qa.a: Sachin could have built a few quiet allies who trust Sachin's work, as Bhavna did, before any crisis, and kept clear records.

qa.q: What might Bhavna have been thinking when Bhavna said, “The records are clean. I checked them”?
qa.a: Bhavna probably wanted to be fair and speak from the evidence, though nobody else in the review would.

grounding: An employee tries to stay out of rival camps, is pressed by both and is left unprotected without clear, quiet allies.

passage: At the cooperative dairy office in a small town near Anand, two camps had formed: those loyal to the old secretary and those backing the new chairman. Farhan, the young accounts clerk, kept his head down and ate lunch alone at his desk. It didn't work. On Monday, the secretary's men asked him to delay the chairman's expense files. On Tuesday, the chairman's nephew asked him to 'find something' in the secretary's accounts. Farhan said no to both, politely. By Thursday, neither side greeted him, and his leave application had been 'lost'. That evening Sumit, the older milk-testing officer, sat beside him at the bus stand. 'You did right. But you need people who know it. Talk to the auditor, and keep copies of every request.' Farhan nodded, feeling less alone.

qa.q: What did the chairman's nephew ask Farhan to do?
qa.a: To 'find something' in the secretary's accounts.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel by Thursday?
qa.a: He felt isolated and unprotected, with neither side greeting him and his leave application 'lost'.

qa.q: What did Sumit suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Talking to the auditor and keeping copies of every request, so Farhan's neutrality has quiet allies and a record to protect him.

qa.q: How might the secretary's men see Farhan's polite refusal?
qa.a: They likely see it as disloyalty rather than principle, which is why they stop greeting him.

grounding: A clerk who stays out of two rival camps is pressed by both and left unprotected until a quiet ally advises him.

passage: At the architecture firm in Melbourne, the two senior partners had stopped speaking, and every junior was expected to pick a side. Mei didn't. She worked on projects for both, answered both politely and skipped the Friday drinks where each camp gathered. For a while she felt proud of it. Then the hospital project ran late, each partner blamed the other's team, and both named Mei as the one who had dropped the ball. Neither defended her. That night she sat in the car park, gripping the steering wheel. Jamal, from the planning team, knocked on the window. 'I saw the emails. You weren't the delay. Want me to go through the timeline with you and the office manager tomorrow?' Mei let out a long breath. 'Yes. Please.'

qa.q: Which project ran late?
qa.a: The hospital project.

qa.q: What does Mei gripping the steering wheel suggest?
qa.a: She felt hurt, alone and trapped, blamed by both partners with no one defending her.

qa.q: What does Mei need now, and how is Jamal offering it?
qa.a: A clear, quiet ally; Jamal offers to go through the timeline with her and the office manager to show she wasn't the delay.

qa.q: What might Jamal see that the partners ignore?
qa.a: Jamal has read the emails and sees that Mei wasn't the delay, and that her neutrality left her without protection.

grounding: An employee staying out of a partners' feud is blamed by both sides and needs a quiet ally with the facts.

passage: On Ward 6 of the district hospital, the two senior sisters had been feuding since the new duty roster. Sister Grace's nurses took the morning tea break together; Sister Philomena's took theirs after. Urmila, a staff nurse in her second year, drank her tea standing at the medicine trolley, belonging to neither group. On Wednesday, Grace asked her to report that Philomena's shift had left the drug register unsigned. On Thursday, Philomena asked her to say Grace had swapped shifts without permission. Urmila said she would only report what she had seen herself. Both sisters went cold, and her night shifts somehow doubled. Uma, the ward clerk, noticed the roster and quietly showed Urmila how to request a formal review through the nursing superintendent. 'Put it in writing,' Uma said. 'Neutral is safer on paper.'

qa.q: Where did Urmila drink her tea?
qa.a: Standing at the medicine trolley.

qa.q: What might Urmila be feeling after both sisters went cold?
qa.a: Likely anxious and exposed, since her principled neutrality brought doubled night shifts and no protection.

qa.q: How does Uma's advice help Urmila?
qa.a: Requesting a formal roster review in writing through the nursing superintendent gives Urmila protection and a record, instead of relying on either camp.

qa.q: How might Sister Grace see Urmila's refusal?
qa.a: Grace likely sees it as siding with Philomena, since in a feud neutrality can look like disloyalty.

grounding: A nurse who refuses to join either side of a ward feud is squeezed by both and needs a quiet ally and a written record.

passage:
Dear Preeti,
When I left college you told me to stay out of office wars. I'm trying. It's harder than you made it sound.
Our design team has split in two since the new head arrived. Aslam's side wants the old process; Karan's side wants the new tool. I told both I'd work with whatever we decide. Now Aslam's people stop talking when I walk into the pantry, and Karan copied me on an email "for my support" that I never gave.
Last week, when the release slipped, both camps pointed at my module. Nobody defended it. I felt proud of staying fair, and completely alone.
I'm not going to pick a side. But I think I need two or three people who know my work and will say so quietly. Is that politics, or just sense?
Write when you can,
Pankaj

qa.q: What did Karan do that Pankaj never agreed to?
qa.a: Karan copied Pankaj on an email "for my support" that Pankaj never gave.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel when both camps blamed the module?
qa.a: Pankaj felt proud of staying fair but also completely alone, because nobody defended the work.

qa.q: What would you advise Pankaj about finding allies?
qa.a: Build quiet trust with a few colleagues who see the work directly and can vouch for its quality, without joining either camp.

qa.q: How might Aslam's side see Pankaj's neutrality?
qa.a: They may read it as secretly siding with Karan, especially after that email, which is why they fall silent in the pantry.

grounding: Pankaj's email shows an employee staying out of rival camps, getting pressed by both, and seeing the need for quiet allies.
